source.title: Scaling Law for Time Series Forecasting
source.authors: Jing-Zhe Shi; Qin-Wei Ma; Huan Ma; Lei Li

record.tranche_reason: The study extends scaling-law experiments to time-series forecasting and reports dataset-size and model-width scaling results. It does not reproduce language-model pretraining experiments.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own scaling results in Figures 1 and 2. It does not measure language-model held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute scaling in language models, or compute-optimal parameter-token allocation. Results from cited work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains time-series forecasting models (NLinear/MLP, ModernTCN, iTransformer) on growing data fractions and widths. It fits loss = A + B/x^α to its own MSE results, so it bears on V5's claim that the power-law form holds in other modalities. It runs no language-model experiments, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 as stated for language models are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors propose an intrinsic-space theory of time-series scaling. Empirically they confirm power-law-like scaling with dataset size, and with model width when the model is not already powerful enough. They find an optimal look-back horizon that grows with training data and depends less on model size. They recommend comparing models at each model's optimal horizon.
record.recipe_differences: Time-series forecasting experiments using forecasting loss (MSE in the experiments), dataset-size and model-width sweeps, and varied look-back horizons; not language-model held-out cross-entropy or parameter/token/compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported width-scaling behavior depends on whether the model is already powerful enough and on data availability; ModernTCN on ETTm1 is reported as an overfitting exception.

fits_no_version.finding: An optimal look-back horizon exists at each data amount and grows with more training data. Larger models can shift the optimum to shorter horizons (Figures 3, 4, 6). Downsampling can improve loss (Figure 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling input context or data granularity does not monotonically reduce loss when data is limited; the optimal context length grows with dataset size.

record.problems: The authors note that their datasets are small relative to recently proposed large datasets, their experiments focus mainly on in-domain forecasting rather than pretrained-then-finetuned or foundation models, and their results depend on assumptions in the theory. They report only one iteration for the largest datasets.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 3–7 report look-back-horizon, model-size/horizon interaction, and downsampling results; these do not measure the claim versions tested here. Appendix I compares alternative curve formulas, but the paper does not state a conclusion about language-model exponents or compute-optimal allocation from those comparisons.

untested.parts: Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are untested, as are time-series foundation models or mixed-dataset training at scale; the authors state their focus is in-domain. Compute scaling is untested. It is also untested whether the power law holds over several orders of magnitude or extrapolates.
Not tested: there are no language-model experiments.
Not tested: there are no extrapolation tests from small to large runs.
Not tested: there is no compute-optimal allocation.
Not tested: there are no fixed-parameter shape comparisons.
Not tested: there are no downstream tasks.
Not tested for language-model laws. The fits do vary by model type and look-back horizon, but no published laws are compared.

missing.what: AIC/BIC comparison of A+B/x^α against pure power law, log and quadratic fits, per model and dataset. The offset power law wins in most cells but not all: on iTransformer ETTh2, g1/g2 have AIC -57.9 vs f -56.9; on MLP ETTh1, g3 ties f at -89.1. rows_left_out declares this appendix but wrongly says it does not bear on the tested versions; it bears on V5's functional form.

Further data-scaling curves for iTransformer on Traffic, NormMLP and NLinear. The authors say the data-dense limit gives a D exponent of -1 and that channel-independent and channel-dependent models sit in different regimes. rows_left_out groups this figure with the horizon figures, but it is a data-scaling result.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Evidence for V5 is mostly figure-only plus the authors' textual statement, with AIC/BIC tables in Appendix I. Models and datasets are small, at about 10^3 GPU-hours total, and Traffic/ECL use one seed. The fits include an irreducible offset A.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining loss and scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits from small language-model runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token counts at fixed compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count in language models.
The study tests dataset-size and model-width scaling for time-series forecasting, but not image/video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream language-model task performance or its relationship to pretraining loss.
Language-model scaling exponents, compute-optimal splits, or their dependence on language-model setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: NLinear/MLP, ModernTCN and iTransformer (reported as a group)
rows.operation_detail: Varied available dataset size and fitted loss(D) = A + B/D^αD.

conditions.value: ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Traffic and Weather; the paper also reports experiments on Exchange, ECL and Electricity
The text states that the fit works across all listed models and datasets; individual curve values are shown in Figure 1

rows.note: The authors explicitly state that the dataset-scaling results fit the stated power-law form across the tested models and datasets. This is an aggregate textual result; the plotted values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The scale range is small: training sets run from fractions of about 8.5k to 37k points. Values are figure-only, so how many orders of magnitude the fit spans cannot be read. The datasets condition lists Exchange/ECL, but the Section 4.1 text names only ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2, Traffic and Weather.

rows.subject: NLinear/MLP, ModernTCN and iTransformer (reported as a group)
rows.size_stated: Model width varied; specific widths not stated in the main text.
rows.operation_detail: Varied model width and fitted loss(W) = A + B/W^α.

conditions.value: Text describes the fit for models that are not powerful enough; individual curve values are shown in Figure 2

rows.note: The reported power-law fit is conditional: it applies when the model is not already sufficiently powerful.
rows.check: Correct. The fit is stated only for models 'not powerful enough' with large data, which is the regime where data is not the bottleneck. Width scaling uses single-hidden-layer MLP, 1–2 block iTransformer and ModernTCN channel dimension.

rows.subject: ModernTCN
rows.size_stated: Model width varied; specific widths not stated in the main text.
rows.note: The text says a large model may overfit and hurt performance in this case.
rows.check: Loss rises with width, the opposite of beneficial scaling. It occurs only under scarce data, where data is the bottleneck, so it qualifies scope rather than contradicting the power-law form. The authors cite this one case as an example ('like ModernTCN for ETTm1'). Values are figure-only.

relationships.condition: Dataset-size scaling for NLinear/MLP, ModernTCN and iTransformer on ETT, Traffic and Weather
relationships.reason: The authors state loss = A + B/D^α fits well for all models and datasets (r1). The Appendix I AIC/BIC tables mostly favour this form over pure power-law, log and quadratic fits.
relationships.display_finding: Loss fitted A+B/D^α across all tested models and datasets, with AIC and BIC mostly favoring this form over pure power-law, logarithmic and quadratic alternatives.

relationships.condition: Width scaling with large data, models not yet able to fit the data
relationships.reason: The authors state loss = A + B/W^α fits well in this regime (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Loss fitted A+B/W^α while models remained unable to fit the available data.

relationships.condition: Width scaling under scarce data (ModernTCN on ETTm1)
relationships.reason: Larger width can overfit and raise loss, so width scaling breaks when data is the bottleneck (r3). The scaled range is also small and read only from figures.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing width could increase loss through overfitting when training data were scarce.
